attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The revision restores all the parts: debt, electronics prices, 'most' of the market, 'parts' of the economy, and GPU concentration and nonuse 'for the most part'. It is a firm compound observation.

contract.note: The plain readings are ordinary: $200B+ of debt, price pressure across categories rather than every product, majority market dependence, and majority nonuse. The 'most of the market' weighting is an evaluator choice, but a reasonable one. Every part must hold for support.

evidence.note: Kiplinger contributor piece, available before the cutoff. It reports $165B of hyperscaler investment-grade issuance in H1 2026 and about $500B over a year. That points toward the debt part, but it is a secondary estimate with no matching issuer universe, and it says nothing on the other parts.
J.P. Morgan AM on Q2 earnings: AI capex drives profits, and semis are about 20% of S&P market cap. Importance to earnings is not majority dependence of market value on GPU sales.
J.P. Morgan summary dated August 2026 on AI-driven memory scarcity and inflation effects. It has no broad electronics price measure and does not address the other parts.

reviews.rationale: This is a compound claim. The debt part looks plausible: e1 cites about $500B of hyperscaler long-term debt in a year. But the packet does not establish pervasive electronics price inflation, majority market dependence, or majority GPU nonuse among the dominant buyers. Nothing contradicts any part either. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his post. He cites the figure from linked reporting but asserts it as his own.

semantics.note: Keeps the $290B figure, 'outside of hyperscalers', and 'vast majority of these deals' being project financing. 'Will go towards building' is a use-of-proceeds remark, not a scorable forecast. 'May or may not exist' describes customer risk, not the speaker's own hedge.

contract.note: Year-to-date through the post date, data-centre debt excluding direct hyperscaler issuance, and deal-count share with dollar share also reported: all ordinary readings. It also correctly says a differently scoped total cannot alone contradict.

evidence.note: Yahoo report of Goldman's $489B AI-related issuance, about 40% from hyperscalers. The remainder is about $293B through July, but it is broader AI-ecosystem debt, not a data-centre-only tally, and it gives no project-finance share.
Goldman strategist transcript: nearly $500B of AI-related debt, hyperscalers 40%. This confirms the broader scope; it has no data-centre breakdown or financing-structure share.
JLL describes an active project-finance construction lending market across tenant credit tiers. It does not measure what share of the issuance is project-financed.

reviews.rationale: The $290B figure roughly matches Goldman's non-hyperscaler remainder, but that remainder covers all AI-related debt, not just data-centre debt. The contract says a scope mismatch does not settle the claim either way. No evidence gives the project-finance share of deals. Neither support nor contradiction is established.

attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast in his post.

semantics.note: 'Are going to be burdened... at the very least' is firm, unhedged language, so it is a scored forecast. It keeps 'for years to come' and 'whether or not capacity turns into revenue'. The normalisation drops 'onerous' but keeps the depreciation-or-write-offs alternative.

contract.note: Reading it as a severe, persistent burden relative to earnings across the major hyperscalers is fair. One caveat: the contract says an unknown accounting basis bars a money assessment. That could block scoring indefinitely, unless GAAP statements are later accepted as the clarified basis.

evidence.note: Alphabet's Q1 2026 call mentions a depreciation headwind. It predates the forecast and is not evidence of a severe multiyear burden.
Microsoft FY27 Q1 results, released on the evaluation date: earnings above expectations. One quarter on a different metric cannot settle a multiyear depreciation forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The early-resolution rule needs several years of post-publication results showing a severe recurring burden. Only one quarter has passed since the post, so the forecast cannot be scored yet. Microsoft's strong quarter does not contradict it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own causal assertion in his post.

semantics.note: It captures the $1.3T figure and the causal claim of demand distortion. It drops the stated mechanisms ('in part' capital, 'in part' ridiculous demands), which is a minor omission that does not change what is tested.

contract.note: Reading distortion as apparent demand materially exceeding credible funded future usage fits the post's argument that backlogs reflect the labs' ability to sign contracts. The contract also requires an approximate amount reconciliation. Both readings are fair.

evidence.note: UBP analysis, dated before the post: OpenAI and Anthropic are estimated at more than $1.25T in compute commitments. That is close to $1.3T, but it is an analyst estimate with no contract reconciliation and no proof of distortion.

reviews.rationale: An analyst estimate puts the commitments near the stated scale. But nothing reconciles the binding obligations, and nothing shows the commitments inflate apparent demand beyond credible funded usage. Nothing contradicts the claim either. The causal claim cannot be settled on this packet.
